# Grounded generator pilot -- AIMS-F

**Section 4 of the grounded-generator brief. Measured, not asserted.** Generated by
`scripts/gen-grounded-items.mjs` against `ISO/IEC 42001:2023` and formatted by
`scripts/emit-pilot-report.mjs` from `PILOT-GROUNDED-AIMSF-3.json`. Nothing in the live bank was touched: this
was a dry run, and the artifact is what `--apply --from=` would insert item for item.

## What the numbers are

| | |
|---|---|
| model | `claude-opus-5` |
| items attempted | 40, allocated across the domains by `weight_pct` |
| items the writer produced | 40 |
| **survivors** | **27** |
| rejected by a code gate | 9 |
| rejected by the blind solver | 4 |
| undecided (solver could not run) | 0 |
| tasks mapped to passages | 34 of 35 |


Allocation is by domain weight rather than evenly over tasks, because that is the basis
`generate-mock-exam` assembles a form on. A pilot spread evenly would over-sample the
light domains and say nothing about the shape of a real form.

## Why items were rejected

A single item can fail more than one gate, so these do not sum to the rejection count.

| n | gate |
|---|---|
| 7 | code: anchor-is-primary |
| 5 | code: reproduction |
| 4 | solver: second defensible option |
| 2 | code: modal-fidelity |

**The options-only probe is not in this table.** It flags; it never rejects. Listing it here
made a check that rejects nothing look like the largest cause of rejection. Its count is in
its own section below.

**`solver COULD NOT RUN` is not a rejection and is never counted as one.** A step that
could not start is not a step that failed: folding it into the rejections would blame the
items for the transport, and folding it into the survivors would clear items nobody checked.

## The gates, and which of them is not a model

| gate | what it checks | model involved |
|---|---|---|
| `clause-exists` | every clause named is in the library, and is not a declared library gap | no |
| `verbatim` | `key_support` occurs **exactly** in the named passage | no |
| `modal-fidelity` | a `must` claim needs a `shall` anchor in a `shall` clause | no |
| `superseded-wording` | retired edition wording anywhere in the item | no |
| `structure` | cue guard, key-as-longest, odd-one-out by negation and by opening word | no |
| `near-duplicate` | share of the **shorter** stem's distinctive terms against live items on the same task | no |
| `shared-distractor-phrase` | a run of 4+ words every distractor carries and the key does not | no |
| `anchor-is-primary` | the key anchors in a **primary** passage of the task, not a supporting one | no |
| `reproduction` | at most a 9-word run shared with any source, in any **served** field | no |
| blind solver | is it solvable to the key from the passages, with no second defensible option | **yes, and it never sees the key** |
| options-only probe | could a candidate with no knowledge pick the key from the option shapes | **yes, and it sees only the options** |

The three gates below the line are new in this run, and each answers a defect the director
found by reading the first pilot:

- **`anchor-is-primary`** takes out the off-task items. Two of the first pilot's survivors
  anchored in a real clause, verbatim, at the right modal strength -- and the clause was not
  what the task examines. Every gate that existed passed them.
- **`shared-distractor-phrase`** takes out the giveaway: three distractors ending in the same
  clause that the stem excludes.
- **`reproduction`** is the gap the first pilot had no gate for at all.

## The paraphrase retry

| | |
|---|---|
| reproduction failures given one retry | 9 |
| **fixed on retry** | **9** |
| still failing after retry | 0 |

The retry is offered for REPRODUCTION ONLY. It is the one failure a rewrite can fix without
changing what the item measures: the claim, the key and the anchor all stay and only our
wording moves. A modal error or a wrong anchor is a different item, so neither is retried.
The offending run is named in the retry -- "paraphrase this" without it rewrites around the
wrong span -- and the result is RE-GATED, never trusted.

## Reproduction in served fields

| | |
|---|---|
| ceiling, stem and options | a run of at most **9** words shared with any source |
| ceiling, explanation | 9 words unquoted, plus ONE attributed quotation of at most one sentence |
| longest served run, max across survivors | 9 |
| median | 5 |
| **survivors over the ceiling** | **0** |

The first pilot had no such gate and **17 of its 31 survivors carried a run of 10 words or
more**, the worst 20. The generator reproduces the standard because it is handed the
standard, which is the cost of grounding and the reason this gate is not optional here.

The runs are measured with the lesson scanner's own tokenisation -- one implementation. The
quotation allowance is a MODE in that module, not a copy. `key_support` is exempt because it
is never served.

**And the index is wider than the library.** The scanner holds nine documents, including
ISO/IEC 22989, 27000, 27004 and 27005, which the task map does not use. One rejection in this
run is a 16-word run against **22989:2022** -- a standard no passage was supplied from, so the
item reproduced it from recall while writing about something else. Scoring against the wider
index is deliberate: the ceiling is about what a candidate can recognise, and recognition does
not care which document we happened to map.

## Anchor clusters -- flagged, not rejected

Items in **different tasks** whose keys rest on the **same clause**. A candidate who reads
one learns the answer to the others, and stem identity cannot see it -- their stems differ,
which is exactly why the deployed dedupe misses them.

| clause | survivors | tasks |
|---|---|---|
| 4.1 | 2 | 1.2, 2.1 |
| 6.1.3 | 2 | 2.8, 4.2 |
| 7.2 | 2 | 3.1, 3.7 |

Recorded per item as `grounding_family`. **`generate-mock-exam` is not touched**, by
instruction; migration 376 adds the column so the assembler can dedupe on it if you rule that way.

## The options-only probe

A third model call on the survivors, seeing the four option texts and **nothing else** -- no
stem, no passages, no key. It flags an item a candidate with zero knowledge could answer from
the shape of the options. It never rejects: with four options it is right one time in four by
luck, so a flag needs both the key AND a concrete, checkable cue.

| | |
|---|---|
| survivors probed | 27 |
| **flagged** | **21** |
| probe could not run | 0 |

> **THIS RATE IS A DESIGN ERROR IN THE REPORT, NOT 21 FINDINGS.** 78 percent of survivors
> flagged. This repository's own rule is that a guard firing on the normal case gets deleted
> by the first person it inconveniences, and that a firing count above a stated threshold is
> a design error rather than a backlog of fixes. So the members were read before the number
> was reported.

> **AND READING THEM FOUND ONE PATTERN, NOT 21.** 6 of the 21 cues describe the same thing:
> the generator makes a distractor wrong by ADDING AN ABSOLUTE OR RESTRICTIVE QUALIFIER, or a
> self-justifying "because..." clause, and leaves the key as the plain statement. That is one
> habit of the writer prompt, and it is exploitable without knowing the subject.

> **The remedy is the one you ruled: rewrite the cue out.** Not a harder gate, not trickery,
> not a longer stem. It belongs in the writer prompt -- tell it not to manufacture a wrong
> answer by qualifying a right one -- and that is a change to what the generator ACCEPTS, so
> it is not made here. The remaining 15 cues are parallelism and length, listed below.

## Survivors

Each shows the anchor the item points at. **`key_support` is internal**: it is a sentence
copied out of a licensed standard as the evidence that the item is supported, and it is
never shown to a candidate, returned by a function, or served through MCP.

### 1. AIMS-F · D1 · task 1.1

**A certification candidate is asked what the elements of an organization's management system are, using the defined term in the vocabulary clause. Which set of elements fits that definition?**

- a) Design and architecture specifications, data descriptions and validation records
- **`KEY` b) Its structure, the assigned roles and responsibilities, planning and operation**
- c) Error rates, processing durations and other agreed performance metrics
- d) Identification, analysis, evaluation and treatment of potential consequences

*explanation:* The vocabulary entry for management system (clause 3.4) describes interrelated elements used to set policies, objectives and processes, and its second note states: "The management system elements include the organization’s structure, roles and responsibilities, planning and operation." The other sets are artefacts or activities of particular technical or assessment controls, not the constituent elements of a management system.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 3.4:*

> The management system elements include the organization’s structure, roles and responsibilities, planning and operation.

*blind solver:* answered B, no second defensible option — Clause 3.4 Note 2 states "The management system elements include the organization's structure, roles and responsibilities, planning and operation."

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (3) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 6 words in the option b  (ceiling 9)  plus one 14-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* 3.4   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (grammar)**

### 2. AIMS-F · D1 · task 1.2

**A firm licenses a machine learning platform from a vendor, integrates it into a diagnostic service it sells to clinics, supplies the training data itself, and also runs the same service on its own staff records. Working through clause 4.1, what should the firm conclude about its position relative to this AI system?**

- **`KEY` a) It can hold several of the listed roles, and its roles can bear on which requirements and controls apply.**
- b) Its integration and data-supply activities place it among AI customers, a category separate from AI partners.
- c) Deciding its role relative to its AI systems is recommended practice for context setting rather than a stated obligation.
- d) Obligations attached to the categories of data it processes sit outside the matters that can inform its role.

*explanation:* Clause 4.1 lists role categories that an organization may occupy 'one or more of', and states that "The organization’s roles can determine the applicability and extent of applicability of the requirements and controls in this document." So multiple simultaneous roles are possible and they influence applicability.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 4.1:*

> The organization’s roles can determine the applicability and extent of applicability of the requirements and controls in this document.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 4.1 states roles "can include... one or more of the following" and that "the organization's roles can determine the applicability and extent of applicability of the requirements and controls in this document."

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (1) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 4 words in the option c  (ceiling 9)  plus one 19-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* 4.1   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (odd-verdict)**

### 3. AIMS-F · D1 · task 1.4

**An organization holds an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and is now planning an AI management system. Its project lead asks why Annex D suggests the two can be run together with relatively little friction. Which explanation reflects Annex D?**

- **`KEY` a) The two standards share the same high-level clause framework, which eases their combined use.**
- b) The information security controls of the AI management system fall away once ISO/IEC 27001 is certified.
- c) ISO/IEC 27001 is cited among the normative references, so its clauses already form part of this document.
- d) The AI management system treats security from a technology-neutral angle, so ISO/IEC 27001 adds little.

*explanation:* Annex D.2 attributes the ease of joint use to the shared high-level structure: "Given that both ISO/IEC 27001 and the AI management systems use the high-level structure, their integrated use is facilitated and of great benefit for the organization." (D.2)

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause D.2:*

> Given that both ISO/IEC 27001 and the AI management systems use the high-level structure, their integrated use is facilitated and of great benefit for the organization.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — D.2 states that 'Given that both ISO/IEC 27001 and the AI management systems use the high-level structure, their integrated use is facilitated and of great benefit for the organization.'

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (17) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 6 words in the option b  (ceiling 9)  plus one 26-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* D.2   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (odd-verdict)**

### 4. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.1

**A medical-imaging firm builds a triage model and also resells a third party's model under its own brand. Preparing the AIMS, the team copies its existing ISO/IEC 27001 context register, which lists market pressures, legal duties and threat trends. Applying Clause 4.1, what does the firm still have to add to satisfy the requirement?**

- **`KEY` a) A determination of the positions the firm occupies in relation to each AI system it supplies or uses**
- b) A documented list of necessary controls with reasons for including or leaving out each one
- c) A record of what system information the firm is obliged to report to parties outside it
- d) An appraisal of machine-learning security concerns that go past conventional system security

*explanation:* Clause 4.1 states: "The organization shall determine its roles with respect to these AI systems." Role determination (provider, producer, customer, partner, and so on) is a Clause 4.1 obligation that an information-security context analysis does not produce.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 4.1:*

> The organization shall determine its roles with respect to these AI systems.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 4.1 explicitly states "The organization shall determine its roles with respect to these AI systems" (e.g. AI provider, producer, customer), which a generic ISO/IEC 27001 context register would not contain.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 4 words in the option a  (ceiling 9)  plus one 12-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* 4.1

### 5. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.2

**A retailer runs three AI-enabled capabilities: a model its data team built, a customer-service suite whose vendor has switched on a generative assistant, and a purchased rostering package with an embedded scoring engine. The AI governance lead is preparing the boundary statement for the AI management system. Which step best fits the requirement for setting that boundary?**

- **`KEY` a) Fix the boundary and its applicability using the internal and external issues and the relevant party requirements already identified, and hold the result as documented information.**
- b) Fix the boundary around the model built in-house, treating the vendor assistant and the embedded scoring engine as the suppliers' management responsibility.
- c) Fix the boundary around the in-house model and record the reasoning for leaving the two purchased capabilities out in the statement of applicability.
- d) Fix the boundary only after designated management has approved the risk treatment plan and accepted the residual risks arising from the purchased capabilities.

*explanation:* Clause 4.3 has the organization settle the boundaries and applicability of the system by weighing the context issues identified under 4.1 together with the interested-party requirements identified under 4.2, and keeping the resulting scope as documented information. Capability bought in, or switched on by a vendor, is still AI the organization uses, so it cannot be pushed outside the boundary as a supplier matter.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 4.3:*

> When determining this scope, the organization shall consider: — the external and internal issues referred to in 4.1; — the requirements referred to in 4.2.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 4.3 requires the organization to determine boundaries and applicability considering the 4.1 internal/external issues and 4.2 interested party requirements, with the scope available as documented information.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (1) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 6 words in the explanation  (ceiling 9)   *anchor family:* 4.3   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (shared-phrase)**

### 6. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.4

**A provider organization has named owners for risk management, security, privacy, data quality and impact assessment work, and has told staff who each owner is. Reviewing this against the leadership requirements of the AI management system standard, which gap should be flagged?**

- **`KEY` a) An owner is still needed for confirming the system meets the document and for briefing leadership on how it performs.**
- b) The set of assignments is complete once every area listed in the Annex B guidance has a named owner.
- c) The governing body, rather than top management, carries the duty to allocate and make known these roles.
- d) An owner for keeping records of each completed impact assessment is the one outstanding leadership allocation.

*explanation:* Clause 5.3 goes beyond assigning and communicating roles in general: top management has to place with someone the responsibility and authority for confirming that the management system meets the document's requirements, and for "reporting on the performance of the AI management system to top management" (5.3). Neither of those two outcomes is owned in the scenario described.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 5.3:*

> Top management shall assign the responsibility and authority for: a) ensuring that the AI management system conforms to the requirements of this document; b) reporting on the performance of the AI management system to top management.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 5.3 requires top management to assign responsibility and authority for ensuring the AI management system conforms to the document and for reporting on its performance to top management, which is missing from the listed assignments.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 5 words in the stem  (ceiling 9)  plus one 12-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* 5.3   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (length)**

### 7. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.5

**A lender is adapting its existing IT risk method to cover a new credit-scoring model. Today, each identified risk is scored only for its effect on service availability and on the confidentiality of customer records, and the scored risks are then ranked. A reviewer notes that the analysis step does not yet meet the AIMS requirement. What should be added to the analysis step?**

- **`KEY` a) Appraisal of what materialisation would mean for the organisation, for individuals and for society**
- b) Checking each proposed safeguard against the reference controls listed in Annex A of the standard
- c) Securing approval from the designated management for the residual exposure that will be carried
- d) Measuring each scored risk against the criteria the organisation has established and maintained

*explanation:* Clause 6.1.2 d) 1) requires the analysis to "assess the potential consequences to the organization, individuals and societies that would result if the identified risks were to materialize". A purely IT-oriented analysis that looks only at availability and confidentiality of the organisation's own data misses the consequences to individuals and to societies that the AIMS analysis step must cover.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.2:*

> d) analyses the AI risks to: 1) assess the potential consequences to the organization, individuals and societies that would result if the identified risks were to materialize;

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 6.1.2 d) 1) requires the analysis to assess the potential consequences to the organization, individuals and societies if identified risks materialize, which a purely availability/confidentiality scoring omits.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 7 words in the option c  (ceiling 9)  plus one 20-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* 6.1.2   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (grammar)**

### 8. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.6

**A provider launched a hiring recommendation tool two years ago and completed an impact assessment at that time. The tool is now being extended to a new country and to a much larger applicant pool, and a separate privacy impact assessment has been prepared for that country. Under the AI management system requirements, how should the team handle the AI system impact assessment?**

- **`KEY` a) Repeat the assessment for the proposed change and retain documented information on the outcome.**
- b) Repeat the assessment once a regulatory authority asks to see the results of the earlier one.
- c) Treat the privacy impact assessment prepared for the new country as covering the extended tool.
- d) Repeat the assessment after applicants report that the extended tool has disadvantaged them.

*explanation:* Clause 8.4 ties performance of the assessment to planned intervals and to proposed significant changes, and requires records of the results: "The organization shall perform AI system impact assessments according to 6.1.4 at planned intervals or when significant changes are proposed to occur." Extending the tool to a new jurisdiction and population is such a proposed change, so the assessment is redone in advance and its results are kept as documented information.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 8.4:*

> The organization shall perform AI system impact assessments according to 6.1.4 at planned intervals or when significant changes are proposed to occur. The organization shall retain documented information of the results of all AI system impact assessments.

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 8.4 requires AI system impact assessments to be performed per 6.1.4 at planned intervals or when significant changes are proposed, and documented information of the results retained.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (6) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 5 words in the stem  (ceiling 9)  plus one 22-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* 8.4   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (shared-phrase)**

### 9. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.7

**A provider has completed and documented an assessment of the consequences that a new hiring tool's rollout, planned use and predictable misuse could have on applicants and on wider society in the jurisdictions where it will run. The AI objectives and risk criteria were fixed earlier. Under ISO/IEC 42001, what is required next for this system?**

- **`KEY` a) Carry the documented consequences into the risk analysis, then determine and rank the resulting risk levels for treatment.**
- b) Accept the documented consequences as satisfying the risk analysis obligation for this particular system.
- c) Divide the two exercises so that risk work covers harm to the organization and the other covers harm to people.
- d) Take the outcome of the risk analysis into account while the consequence assessment is being prepared and documented.

*explanation:* Clause 6.1.4 makes the impact assessment an input to risk work: “The organization shall consider the results of the AI system impact assessment in the risk assessment (see 6.1.2).” The risk assessment itself still has to run under 6.1.2, analysing consequences and likelihood, determining levels of risk and prioritizing them against the risk criteria for treatment.

*`key_support` — ISO/IEC 42001 clause 6.1.4:*

> The organization shall consider the results of the AI system impact assessment in the risk assessment (see 6.1.2).

*blind solver:* answered A, no second defensible option — Clause 6.1.4 requires the organization to consider the impact assessment results in the risk assessment, and 6.1.2 d)–e) then requires analysing consequences, determining levels of risk and prioritizing them for treatment.

*gates:* clause-exists pass (4) · verbatim pass (4) · modal-fidelity pass (1) · superseded-wording pass (6) · structure pass (4) · near-duplicate pass (18) · shared-distractor-phrase pass (3) · anchor-is-primary pass (2) · reproduction pass (6)

*longest served run:* 5 words in the option c  (ceiling 9)  plus one 18-word attributed quotation in the explanation   *anchor family:* 6.1.4   **OPTIONS-PROBE FLAG (length)**

### 10. AIMS-F · D2 · task 2.8

**An AI governance team has chosen its treatment options, worked out the controls needed, checked them against the Annex A reference list, and drafted both the statement of applicability and the treatment plan. Before the planning stage can be regarded as complete, which action is still outstanding?**

- **`KEY` a) Obtain sign-off from the management designated for it, covering the plan and the acceptance of leftover risk.**
- b) Obtain sign-off from the governing body for the risk criteria before the draft plan is circulated further.
- c) Record in the statement of applicability a reason for each item of Annex B guidance left out of scope.
- d) Keep documented results of the finished treatment activities on file before the plan is put into effect.

*explanation:* Clause 6.1.3 closes the treatment process with an approval step: "The organization shall obtain approval from the designated management for the AI risk treatment plan and for acceptance of the residual AI risks." The other options misplace the actor, the object of documentation, or the sequence.

that needs reading.

## What this pilot does not show

- **Tier A and Tier B rates are a HUMAN READ, and this report is not one.** The target was
  zero Tier A and a Tier B rate well under 9%. Nothing here can claim either: a Tier A
  finding is a wrong key, and the instrument that establishes a key is wrong is somebody
  reading the item against the standard. What the gates establish is narrower and worth
  saying exactly: every survivor points at a real sentence in a pinned edition, the
  sentence says what the item claims it says at the strength the item claims, and a model
  that never saw the key reached the key from the passages alone.
- **A DEFINITION CLAUSE'S `normative` CLASS IS THE WEAKEST THING IN THE LIBRARY.** The
  extractor classes a passage by the strongest modal in its own text, which is right for a
  requirement clause and crude for a terms-and-definitions entry: a definition whose note
  contains the word *can* is classed `can`, and a definition imposes nothing at all. One
  rejection in this run turns on that (clause 3.2). Refusing is still the right direction --
  an item may not say *should* on the authority of a definition -- but the class is a proxy
  and `informative` would describe those rows better.
- **The near-duplicate gate compares stems.** Two items with different stems and the same
  answer are invisible to it -- which is exactly the eight near-duplicate pairs the
  480-item audit found by reading. A threshold cannot find those.
- **A dry run of a generator is a sample, not a preview.** A second run writes different
  items. These are the items that were gated, because the artifact was persisted first.
- **The library is PARTIAL where it says so.** No item was refused for naming a missing clause in this run.

## The comparison the decision actually needs

This report cannot be read against the old generator on its own. The old path's error rate
is known from a human read -- 16 wrong keys in 822 items, 1.9% -- and the equivalent number
for these survivors requires the same instrument: somebody reading them against ISO/IEC
42001:2023. The survivors above are laid out in `AUDIT-SAMPLE.md`'s format so that read can
happen the same way, and each one carries the sentence it rests on so the reading is against
the standard's own words rather than against recall.
